title: Supercooled kidneys have been transplanted into pigs in a “landmark achievement”
gist: A Texas A&M team led by thermodynamicist Matthew Powell Palm kept pig kidneys ice-free at -4 °C under constant pressure for up to 72 hours without cryoprotectants, then autotransplanted them successfully — recovery was faster than the 24-hour cold-ice standard, and pigs stayed healthy for up to 200 days. Because the method uses no chemical cryoprotectants, the team hopes for accelerated FDA clearance and plans to launch a company with Sebastian Giwa within months.

insights.claim: A Texas A&M team led by Matthew Powell Palm has built a device that holds organs at -4 °C (25 °F) without any ice forming, by keeping the organ submerged under constant pressure rather than using antifreeze chemicals.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A preservation method with no added chemistry sidesteps the toxicology and approval burden that has stalled cryoprotectant-based competitors, which is the main gating factor on time-to-market.
insights.locator: Matthew Powell Palm at Texas A&M University and his colleagues

insights.claim: Avoiding cryoprotectants is a deliberate regulatory strategy, not just a scientific preference: chemicals used as antifreeze may have side effects and would themselves need approval before use in human transplants.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: The chemistry-free design is the core moat — it converts a drug-approval problem into a device-approval problem, which is faster and cheaper.
insights.locator: By keeping an organ submerged at a constant pressure

insights.claim: The supercooling hardware is deliberately unsophisticated — a hermetically sealed chamber with a transparent lid, a temperature/ice-nucleation monitor at its base, and the same preservation solution already used clinically — with the difficulty living in the kinetics, not the components.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Low bill-of-materials and off-the-shelf preservation solution imply cheap manufacturing and easy scaling if the science holds — the value is in know-how and IP, not in components.
insights.quote: I always describe this as low-tech high science,
insights.locator: The device itself is essentially a hermetically sealed chamber

insights.claim: No one has yet been able to freeze and thaw a human organ for transplantation, despite decades of work on cryoprotectants and varied temperatures, even though cryopreservation of eggs, sperm and embryos is routine.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Defines the unsolved problem the whole field is racing at — supercooling to just below 0 °C is a partial, near-term workaround rather than the full organ-banking prize.
insights.locator: We've long been able to successfully cryopreserve eggs, sperm, and embryos

insights.claim: Pig kidneys supercooled for 24 hours began producing urine immediately on reimplantation and showed normal function markers within roughly 10 days — slower than kidneys on ice for two hours, but much faster than kidneys on ice for 24 hours.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: The comparison that matters commercially is against the 24-hour ice standard, not against fresh organs — and on that benchmark supercooling wins.
insights.locator: Once the 24-hour supercooled kidneys were transplanted

insights.claim: Kidneys supercooled for 48 and 72 hours performed similarly to the 24-hour supercooled group, suggesting the technique does not degrade materially as storage time triples.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A flat damage curve out to 72 hours is what makes long-haul organ logistics and international donation economically plausible.
insights.quote: Even at three days—triple the clinical standard—we’re getting recovery that is faster than … [what has been] the gold standard for the last three decades,
insights.locator: The organs that were kept supercooled for 48 and 72 hours

insights.claim: Transplant surgeon Heidi Yeh of Mass General Brigham for Children notes that in other studies kidneys stored 48 hours typically take a week or two before they start working again, framing the supercooled 10-day recovery as a genuine step change.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Independent expert corroboration from a competing preservation researcher raises the credibility of the result beyond the founders' own claims.
insights.quote: Often kidneys that have been stored for 48 hours [in other studies] take a week or two before they start working again.

insights.claim: Over 30 days the recipient pigs grew about 30% and the single stored-and-reimplanted kidney nearly doubled in size to compensate for growth and the missing second kidney, indicating the organs retained normal adaptive capacity.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Compensatory hypertrophy is a stronger functional endpoint than urine output — it argues the preservation damage is not merely masked in the short term.

insights.claim: One pig was monitored for 200 days before its stored kidney was removed and analysed, and the organ still looked healthy at that point.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Long-horizon histology is the evidence regulators will want; its presence shortens the plausible path to a human trial.
insights.locator: The team monitored one of the pigs for 200 days

insights.claim: The results were presented at the American Transplant Congress in Boston rather than published, so the headline supercooling data has not yet cleared peer review.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Conference-stage evidence is a discount factor when underwriting the venture — watch for the peer-reviewed publication as the de-risking event.
insights.locator: He and his colleagues presented the findings at the American Transplant Congress

insights.claim: More than 104,000 people are waiting for a kidney transplant in the US and an estimated 17 people die every day while waiting, defining the addressable pain point for any preservation technology.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Sizes the market and the political urgency that would support reimbursement and expedited regulatory treatment.

insights.claim: In some years around one in three donated kidneys are discarded, often because they are too degraded by the time they reach a recipient — meaning supply loss, not just donor scarcity, is a large part of the shortage.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A third of existing supply is recoverable without a single new donor — that is the value pool preservation tech captures.
insights.locator: In some years, around one in three donated kidneys end up being discarded

insights.claim: Both current storage modalities — ice at around 4 °C and body-mimicking perfusion devices — cap out at roughly 24 hours, which is often not long enough to find a suitable recipient and move the organ.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: The 24-hour ceiling is the binding constraint on organ logistics; anything that breaks it resets the entire allocation network's geography.
insights.locator: Kidneys can be stored on ice for around 24 hours

insights.claim: Kevin Myer of the Texas organ procurement organization LifeGift argues that moving the practical kidney limit from an assumed 18–24 hours to 72 hours would enable international donation and cheaper transport options.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Second-order effect: cheaper transport modes and cross-border matching would disrupt the regional organ procurement organization structure, not just improve outcomes.
insights.quote: If we can get up to 72 hours … that would change everything.
insights.locator: Those extra hours could make all the difference

insights.claim: A Canadian team earlier this year cooled pig kidneys below zero and transplanted them, but used a cryoprotectant, stored for up to 48 hours, and the organs survived only a week — a materially weaker result than the 72-hour, 30-day-plus supercooling outcome.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Establishes a competitive benchmark: the Texas A&M approach leads on both duration and post-transplant survival while carrying less regulatory baggage.
insights.quote: It’s the first time this has ever been reported in history,
insights.locator: Earlier this year, researchers in Canada showed

insights.claim: Preliminary work has kept organs supercooled for up to 120 hours with the organs still appearing healthy, though none of those have been transplanted yet.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: The 120-hour datapoint is the option value in the story; watch for the first 120-hour transplant as the next proof point.
insights.locator: Powell Palm and his colleagues think they may even be able to go beyond 72 hours

insights.claim: Because the process uses no cryoprotective chemicals, the Texas A&M team is targeting an accelerated approval from the US Food and Drug Administration to begin testing the device in human transplantation.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Regulatory pathway choice is the main binary for timing — accelerated device clearance versus a chemistry-driven review differs by years.
insights.locator: And because the process doesn't require any cryoprotective chemicals

insights.claim: The storage device is compact enough that supercooled kidneys have already been driven across the US in the back of a Kia Sorento, though it has not yet been tested for air travel.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Road-transport stability without air certification is a real near-term commercial constraint — and also a cost advantage if organs can travel by ground rather than charter jet.
insights.quote: From a stability perspective, we view this as an even higher bar.
insights.locator: The storage device is simple and compact

insights.claim: Matthew Powell Palm and colleague Sebastian Giwa plan to launch a company in the coming months dedicated to the supercooling technology and other protocols that “stop biological time.”
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A named near-term company formation is the concrete investable event out of this research; track the raise and which preservation protocols get bundled in.
insights.locator: Powell Palm and his colleague Sebastian Giwa plan to launch a company
